guide.summary: This unit covers current, resistance and resistivity, Ohm's law, electric power, series and parallel combinations, Kirchhoff's rules, real batteries with internal resistance, and circuits with capacitors (steady state and the qualitative behavior of RC circuits). Bulb-brightness reasoning and circuit-analysis derivations appear on almost every exam.

sections.heading: Current, resistance, and power
sections.body: Current I = Δq/Δt is the rate of charge flow; conventional current goes from + to − outside the battery. Resistance R = ρℓ/A depends on resistivity, length, and cross-sectional area (doubling diameter quadruples area). Ohm's law: ΔV = IR for ohmic resistors. Power: P = IΔV = I²R = ΔV²/R. Bulb brightness depends on power dissipated. Current isn't used up: the same current enters and leaves a resistor; energy is transferred.

sections.heading: Series and parallel
sections.body: Series: same current through each element; R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + …; voltages divide in proportion to resistance. Parallel: same potential difference across each branch; 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …; R_eq is less than the smallest branch; currents divide inversely with resistance. Adding a resistor in series increases R_eq and reduces current; adding a branch in parallel decreases R_eq and increases total current from the battery. With an ideal battery, adding a parallel bulb doesn't change the brightness of other parallel bulbs.

sections.heading: Kirchhoff's rules and real batteries
sections.body: Junction rule (charge conservation): current into a junction equals current out. Loop rule (energy conservation): the sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero. A real battery has internal resistance r: terminal voltage ΔV = ε − Ir, which falls as current increases; maximum current (short circuit) is ε/r. Ammeters are placed in series and should have very low resistance; voltmeters in parallel with very high resistance.

sections.heading: Capacitors in circuits
sections.body: Capacitors in parallel: C_eq = C₁ + C₂; in series: 1/C_eq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. In an RC circuit, an uncharged capacitor initially acts like a wire (full current flows); as it charges, current decreases exponentially; at steady state no current flows through the capacitor branch (it acts like an open switch), and the capacitor's voltage equals the voltage across the branch it's connected in parallel with. The time constant τ = RC sets how fast charging occurs.

keyTakeaways: Series: same I; parallel: same ΔV.
P = IΔV = I²R = ΔV²/R; brightness ∝ power.
Steady-state capacitor: no current through its branch.
commonMistakes: Thinking current is used up by bulbs.
Forgetting that doubling diameter quadruples area.
Assuming all bulbs in a circuit have equal brightness.
Treating a fully charged capacitor as a wire.
examTips: Bulb questions: compute or compare current or voltage for each bulb, then power.
Derivations: write the loop rule with symbols before solving.
Lab FRQs often graph R vs. ℓ or ΔV vs. I; relate slope to ρ/A or R.
For capacitor circuits, analyze t = 0 and t → ∞ separately.
guide.cramSheet:
**Basics:** I = Δq/Δt · R = ρℓ/A · ΔV = IR · P = IΔV = I²R = ΔV²/R

**Series:** same I · R_eq = ΣR

**Parallel:** same ΔV · 1/R_eq = Σ1/R

**Kirchhoff:** junction (ΣI_in = ΣI_out) · loop (ΣΔV = 0)

**Battery:** ΔV_terminal = ε − Ir

**Capacitors:** parallel C add · series 1/C add · t = 0 wire · steady state open · τ = RC

practice.prompt: Students want to determine the resistivity of a metal alloy. They have a long wire of the alloy with diameter 0.50 mm, a variable power supply, an ammeter, a voltmeter, connecting clips, and a meterstick.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe a procedure to collect data that would allow the students to determine the resistivity. Include how each instrument is connected and how to reduce experimental uncertainty.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt:
The students' data are:

| Length (m) | 0.20 | 0.40 | 0.60 | 0.80 | 1.00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Resistance (Ω) | 1.1 | 2.3 | 3.3 | 4.5 | 5.6 |

Describe a graph of these data that would yield a straight line, including axis labels with units and a best-fit line.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Use the slope of your best-fit line to calculate the resistivity of the alloy.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The wire heats up noticeably at higher currents. Explain how this would affect the measured resistivity.

rubric.description: Measure length with meterstick; measure current with ammeter in series and voltage with voltmeter in parallel across the length of wire.
Vary the length between clips over several values and calculate R = ΔV/I for each.
Repeat trials, use many lengths, or keep current low to limit heating.
Resistance (Ω) on vertical axis, length (m) on horizontal, linear scales.
Straight line through the data, not forced through every point.
Slope = ρ/A, with A = π(0.25 × 10⁻³ m)² ≈ 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m².
Resistivity of metals increases with temperature, so heating makes measured R and ρ too large.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Connect the power supply, ammeter, and wire in series, using clips to select a length of wire. Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the selected length. Measure the length between the clips with the meterstick. Set a low voltage, record the current and voltage, and calculate R = ΔV/I. Repeat for at least five different lengths, and repeat each measurement several times and average. Keep the current small to avoid heating the wire.

B. Plot resistance (Ω) on the vertical axis and length (m) on the horizontal axis with evenly spaced scales. The five points lie nearly on a straight line; draw a best-fit line through them, which passes near the origin.

C. Slope ≈ (5.6 − 1.1)/(1.00 − 0.20) ≈ 5.6 Ω/m. Since R = ρℓ/A, the slope equals ρ/A. A = π(0.25 × 10⁻³ m)² = 1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m². ρ = (5.6 Ω/m)(1.96 × 10⁻⁷ m²) ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m.

D. The resistivity of a metal increases as its temperature increases, so heating would make the measured resistance, and therefore the calculated resistivity, larger than the room-temperature value.
